[00:00] Jordan (Redwood AE): Hey everyone, thanks for joining. Quick roll call then we'll jump into the run results. Priya and I are here. Anita, you good?
[00:08] Anita (Novapay): Yeah, hi, thanks. Morning. We have Miguel and Samir on the call too. Rosa is here as well.
[00:12] Jordan: Awesome. Last week we ran the sustained load at concurrency 25 with continuous batching off, right? Samir, can you give a quick recap of what you saw?
[00:22] Samir: Yeah so the run was about two hours, mostly steady-state 25 conc, we saw average throughput close to 1.2k reqs per minute but p95 was like 420 ms and p99 spiked to 1.8 to 2.1 seconds on a couple of bursts. There's also increased cpu on the mux instance, and the KV cache didn't look fully warm at the start, so we had some cold hits.
[00:45] Priya (SE): Right, that aligns with what we expected. With continuous batching off, you're not aggregating requests efficiently and the model is getting lots of small micro-batches which bumps token overhead per request. Also the KV cache warm-up means the early requests pay the overhead.
[00:58] Miguel (CTO): Quick question - when you say continuous batching, are we talking about the Redwood runtime feature that keeps the batching window open for a few ms to accumulate requests? We've seen similar in other runtimes, just want to make sure the semantics are the same.
[01:10] Priya: Yes exactly. It's request coalescing with an adaptive window. It trades a few ms of tail latency for much higher throughput and lower cost per token by amortizing kernel launch overhead. For the workloads we saw (short prompts, avg 120 tokens), continuous batching should help a lot.
[01:25] Rosa (Product): We're sensitive to p99 though - our user-facing latencies at checkout need to stay under 400-500 ms ideally. If continuous batching introduces spikes beyond that, it's risky.
[01:35] Priya: Totally - that's why we recommend combining batching with a concurrency target and a small queue/backpressure policy: target concurrency of 35-45, queue depth cap at say 80, and a max latency SLA that triggers falling back to a lower-quality but faster model variant if p99 breaches 800 ms. That keeps the UX safe while maximizing throughput.
[01:53] Anita: Can you explain the queueing/backpressure a bit more? If we cap queue depth, won't requests get dropped?
[02:01] Priya: Good question. They won't be dropped - they'll be rejected with a 429 or routed to a fallback depending on the policy. For the pilot we usually set the routing to: if queue > cap, then route to a cheaper hosted model or return a quick graceful degradation. You can also set an adaptive cap so it increases slightly during predictable batch windows.
[02:20] Samir: For infra notes, we enabled the pod autoscaler, but it was slow to scale because the metric was throughput not queue depth; we should watch latency and queue depth metrics for more proactive scaling. Also need to ensure the GPU instance has enough reserved memory for KV cache so we don't thrash.
[02:40] Priya: Exactly - kernel selection matters too. For your sequence lengths, the runtime will pick different attention kernels; we saw a few CPU fallback paths because the sequence distribution spiked on longer requests. I'll add kernel-level notes in the doc.
[02:54] Miguel: What about quantization? Could that reduce the p99? We already tested int8; we saw quality regressions on some prompts.
[03:05] Priya: Quant helps with throughput and memory, but it can change output distribution. For now we recommend the following: keep fp16 for quality-critical endpoints, test q4_0 as a middle ground for batch-internal pipelines where minor hallucination risk is tolerable. We'll include a recommended quantization profile per route in the notes.
[03:26] Jordan: Ok let's look at the numbers. Jordan shares the throughput spreadsheet link in chat.
[03:30] Speaker 6: got the link.
[03:33] Jordan: So last week's run - average 1.2k rpm, cost estimate X, p95 420 ms, p99 1.9s. With continuous batching on and target concurrency 40, our internal sim projects 2.6k rpm and p95 under 300 ms, p99 around 550-700 ms. Those p99 numbers assume KV cache warmed and queue cap at 80.
[03:58] Anita: Those are promising - 2.6k rpm is close to what we need. But how confident are you in the p99 sims? We need real observed data, not just sim.
[04:08] Priya: Fair. The sim uses historical sequence distribution plus a stochastic model of arrival times. It tends to under-estimate bursts because it assumes Poisson arrivals; real traffic has burstiness. That's why we want you to run a sustained 1-hour test with realish traces and concurrency 40, batching on, and queueing enabled. That will surface corner cases.
[04:28] Samir: On the test infra side, I'll spin up the load agents and replay a 10x burst pattern we saw in production. One ask - can Redwood provide a small agent or script that hits the endpoint with the correct headers and x-request-id so we can match traces?
[04:41] Jordan: Yes, we'll share a load harness script and also a few sample curl commands. We'll include the headers to preserve tracing.
[04:48] Rosa: Another ops question - VPC peering and KMS. We still need to confirm KMS integration for key rotation. The security team flagged HSM support as a must for production.
[04:58] Priya: We support customer-managed KMS and HSM through our Private offering; for Hosted we offer envelope encryption with BYOK options. Priya to follow up with security docs. We'll schedule a security review follow-up next week.
[05:12] Miguel: Can you clarify Dedicated vs Hosted economics at these throughputs? When does Dedicated make sense?
[05:18] Jordan: Short answer: at sustained throughput above ~3k rpm and predictable hours, Dedicated reserved capacity beats hosted on unit cost. But there's an initial commitment. We'll send a pricing comparison for your observed runs.
[05:31] Anita: Back to tuning - Priya, you mentioned KV cache warmers. How do we prevent cold-starts for daily traffic spikes?
[05:39] Priya: Two tactics: proactively pre-warm common prefixes during low-traffic windows and use sticky routing to keep hot sessions on warmed instances. Also the runtime supports a progressive cold-warm threshold so you can accept slightly higher cold misses for infrequent flows. We'll include a script to prime the KV cache.
[05:58] Samir: For the warmers, we need to be careful with costs; if we pre-warm a ton of prefixes it can get pricey. We'll prefer a prioritized list (top N prefixes) - Rosa, maybe product can give top 200 patterns?
[06:10] Rosa: Yep we can generate top 200. We'll send that to Samir this week.
[06:14] Jordan: Cool. Any blockers on running the 1-hour test? Samir?
[06:18] Samir: I need the harness and the exact config - concurrency target, batching window ms, queue cap. If you share those we'll run it tomorrow. Also will attach full traces and host metrics.
[06:28] Jordan: Action: we'll send recommended config. Quick note - set batching window to adaptive, min 2 ms max 12 ms for your workload. Target concurrency 40, queue cap 80, fallback policy route to hosted lite model if p99 > 800 ms.
[06:44] Priya: Also enable the runtime's instrumentation flags to capture kernel path counts and batch-size distribution; that helps us tune kernel selection. It adds negligible overhead.
[06:55] Anita: One more thing - we had a security question about audit logs. Can Redwood provide token-level audit logs with SSO correlation?
[07:03] Jordan: Yes, we have per-token cost and latency breakdowns, and you can ingest audit logs into your SIEM. We'll include the log schema in the security docs.
[07:12] Miguel: Great. If the 1-hr test looks good, what's the next milestone?
[07:16] Jordan: If the test passes thresholds (sustained throughput within 10% of sim, p95 < 350 ms, p99 < 700 ms), we propose a 2-week ramp to a pilot Dedicated config with reserved GPUs, then evaluate pricing and run a production-like 24-hour soak.
[07:31] Rosa: Sounds reasonable.
[07:33] Anita: Do we need legal to sign anything before the 24-hour soak?
[07:37] Jordan: For pilot testing no. For Dedicated reserved capacity will require SOW/contract. We'll bring legal in when you opt for Dedicated.
